extracted.intended_audience: readers and performers of Restoration drama; general readers and scholars of Dryden/theatre history
extracted.subtask_description: Reading, staging, or performing John Dryden's Restoration comedy Marriage A-la-mode (with attention to character portrayal, language/affectation, and period staging/promotional practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of Melantha (the affected lady)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Melantha is as finished an impertinent as ever fluttered in a drawing-room; and seems to contain the most complete system of female foppery that could possibly be crowded into the tortured form of a fine lady. Her language, dress, motion, manners, soul, and body, are in a continual hurry to be something more than is necessary or commendable." (Colley Cibber)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting guidance and concrete beats given by Cibber: read the lover's letter with a careless dropping lip and an erected brow; hum it hastily over; crumble the letter in the palm; 'pour down upon him her whole artillery of airs, eyes, and motion'; collapse the body daintily as if 'sinking under the conscious load of her own attractions'; play the chest forward in 'fifty falls and risings, like a swan upon waving water'; show rapid fondness of her own wit, cutting off the lover's praise; use silent assenting bows and vain endeavours to speak; move quickly between engagements (e.g., 'swims from him to make' visits). Cibber emphasizes fantastical expression and mannered physicality as essential to the character; imitating Mrs Monfort's action was considered the exemplar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of French phrases/linguistic affectation to signal character
rubrics_metrics.description: "Of the French phrases, which the affected lady throws into her conversation, some have been since naturalized, as good graces, minuet, chagrin, grimace, ridicule, and others."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats the insertion of French words as a marked affectation of the 'affected lady' and a performer/writer should use such loan-words to signal coquetry and fashionable pretension. Examples given serve as a short model-list of words that convey affectation; their presence is part of the character's comic identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of comic scenes versus tragic elements (tone consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Little can be said of the tragic part of the drama. The sudden turn of fortune in the conclusion is ridiculed in 'The Rehearsal.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit evaluative standard: abrupt tragic reversals or sudden shifts in tone (particularly at the conclusion) risk undermining the comic effect and invite ridicule. As an anti-pattern, a sudden turn of fortune that clashes with the play's comic register should be avoided or handled carefully to preserve coherence and audience reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging and audience-attraction by following contemporary modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Prologue asserts the company will 'follow the new mode which they begin, / And treat them with a room, and couch within: / For that's one way, howe'er the play fall short, / To oblige the town, the city, and the court.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical standard for producers: adopt fashionable entertainments and social practices (e.g., masking balls, hospitality within the theatre) to recommend and endear a play to audiences across town, city, and court. The prologue frames promotional and staging choices (masquerade, social amenities) as legitimate tactics to secure attendance and favor when the play itself might otherwise underperform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence of acting/characterization as decisive to a play's success
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary testimony: the Gentleman's Magazine praised the first representation as 'made its first appearance with extraordinary lustre' and the verses appended praise the excellence of the original performers (e.g., Mrs Monfort as Melantha). Colley Cibber's remarks treat performance as central to realizing the character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied evaluative criterion: the success of the play depends heavily on 'lively' or exemplary acting—casting appropriate performers for comic parts and executing the physical and verbal mannerisms described (see Melantha entry) are decisive. The historical note that acting troupes and individual performers (named examples such as Mrs Monfort, Woffington, Cibber) could make or break reception serves as guidance to prioritize actor skill, comic timing, and vivid characterization.
